mcqs.question: A card row is signed off at 375px portrait and 768px portrait, where nothing overflows. In landscape on a 390px phone the viewport is 844px wide and the row leaves a large empty gap on the right; in a 500px split-screen pane the third card is clipped. Which conclusion about the validation is correct?
options: The two widths are snapshots: a breakpoint proves nothing about the widths between them or in landscape, so the row must be fluid.
The layout is validated: both common device classes pass, and landscape re-evaluates the same queries that were already verified.
Only widths under 375px remain untested, because the 375px rule covers every narrow screen in either orientation.
Orientation needs no separate coverage: rotation re-runs the media queries, so the landscape check is the portrait check.
mcqs.explanation: A media query is a threshold, not a proof: a rule that passes at 375px and 768px describes the layout at those two widths only, and everything else is whatever the sizing declarations do when the available width changes. This row has no fluid track, so the interval 376-768 and the landscape width (844px on a 390px phone) were never observed, which is exactly why they fail; the repair is a layout whose column count follows the available width - `repeat(auto-fill, minmax())` already covers the widths between breakpoints - validated at narrow, wide and intermediate widths in both orientations (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_grid_layout). The strongest distractor is the 'both device classes pass' one, because a device class is a bucket of widths rather than one width: a 390px phone is 844px wide in landscape and a 500px split pane belongs to no class at all, so passing the bucket's representative width says nothing about its edges. The 375px-rule option fails the same way, since a max-width rule only ever describes what happens below it and the reported failures sit above it. The rotation option confuses re-evaluating a query with covering a width: rotation is precisely how a width that was never checked appears.

mcqs.question: You build a horizontal drag carousel with Pointer Events and start the drag on `pointerdown`. On a phone, a slightly diagonal finger movement makes the page scroll vertically and the carousel stops receiving `pointermove`; calling `preventDefault()` inside the `pointermove` handler changes nothing. What is the correct fix?
options: Declare `touch-action: pan-y` on the carousel so vertical panning stays with the browser and horizontal gestures belong to the drag.
Call `preventDefault()` on every `pointermove` of the drag, so the browser gives up the scroll as soon as the drag starts.
Attach a non-passive `touchstart` listener that cancels touch events on the whole page while a drag is active.
Move the drag listeners to `document` so the browser scroll cannot interrupt the handlers mid-gesture.
mcqs.explanation: Gesture ownership is decided before the gesture starts, and `touch-action` is the declaration that states it: it tells the browser which pans it may still start on that region, so `pan-y` keeps vertical scrolling while the horizontal movement becomes the drag's, and the `pointermove` stream survives (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Pointer_events). The strongest distractor is the `preventDefault()` one, because it sounds like the imperative version of the same intent and it is the first thing people try: by the time `pointermove` fires, the browser has already claimed the pan and is scrolling, so cancelling inside the move handler arrives after the decision it was supposed to stop, which is why the stem reports no change. The page-wide `touchstart` cancel trades one broken gesture for a broken page: it removes scrolling everywhere, needs a per-gesture opt-in to be usable at all, and is the blunt version of a decision that belongs to one region. Moving the listeners to `document` changes where the handler runs, not who owns the gesture — the pan decision is per-element `touch-action`, so the scroll still wins and the carousel still loses the stream.

mcqs.question: During a Pointer Events drag, the pointer moves fast and leaves the element's bounds; pointermove events stop arriving at the original target. What keeps the drag alive?
options: `setPointerCapture(event.pointerId)` at drag start, so later events stay targeted to the element that owns the drag.
A `pointermove` listener on `document` plus manual hit-testing, so no move is missed while the pointer travels.
`touch-action: none` on the page, so the browser never takes the gesture away from the element.
`event.stopPropagation()` in `pointerdown`, so ancestor elements cannot react to the same gesture.
mcqs.explanation: Pointer capture retargets every subsequent event of that pointer to the capturing element, as if hit-testing always resolved to it, so a fast drag keeps producing `pointermove` after the pointer leaves the bounds; it is per `pointerId` and has to be released on `pointerup` and on `pointercancel` (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Pointer_events). The strongest distractor is the document listener with manual hit-testing, because it does receive the moves too: the objection is cost and correctness, not reach. It reimplements what capture already guarantees — hit-testing, `pointerId` bookkeeping and an event that tells you the pointer was lost — with more branches to get wrong, and it still leaves the second decision untouched, because whether the browser may take the gesture at all is a `touch-action` question. `touch-action: none` answers a different question: it is about which pans the browser may perform on that region, not about where events are routed, so events keep hitting whatever is under the pointer (and a page-wide `none` also removes scrolling from the whole page). `stopPropagation()` only stops the event from reaching ancestors; it does not retarget anything, and `pointermove` is delivered to the hit-tested element, not to the drag owner.

mcqs.question: A monitoring config needs the three current Core Web Vitals and the 'good' boundary for each. Which set is correct?
options: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1
FCP ≤ 1.8 s, FID ≤ 100 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1
LCP ≤ 2.5 s, TTI ≤ 3.8 s, CLS ≤ 0.1
LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 500 ms, CLS ≤ 0.25
mcqs.explanation: The current set is LCP for loading, INP for responsiveness and CLS for visual stability, and each 'good' boundary applies to field data at the 75th percentile, segmented by device class rather than read as one aggregate (https://web.dev/articles/vitals). The strongest distractor is the FCP/FID set, because both are real metrics that used to be in the lineup and a dashboard copied from an older article looks authoritative: FID measured the delay of the first input only, INP replaced it as the interactivity signal, and FCP measures a first paint rather than the largest element, so that set would leave the actual loading and interaction experience unmonitored. TTI is a lab-only Lighthouse metric that never belonged to the Core Web Vitals. The last set keeps the right metric names and breaks the boundaries: 500 ms and 0.25 are where INP and CLS turn poor, not where they are good, so a page at 450 ms INP and 0.2 CLS would be reported green while both vitals are failing.

mcqs.question: Field data shows an INP regression on mobile but not on desktop, and you cannot reproduce it on your development machine. What is the correct next step?
options: Segment by device and route, reproduce in the lab with mobile CPU throttling, fix the main cause, then confirm in the field.
Close the ticket: a regression that cannot be reproduced on a development machine is measurement noise, not a real one.
Memoize every component and defer every script, then watch whether the mobile number moves in next week's report.
Report only the desktop score: mobile is a small share of traffic and its percentiles are usually too noisy to act on.
mcqs.explanation: Field data records what real users experienced at the 75th percentile, and your laptop is not their device: the same JavaScript runs several times slower on a low-end Android, so the sequence is segment (which route, which device class, since when), reproduce under comparable conditions in the lab with CPU throttling and a slow network profile, fix the largest contributor, then compare the same segment's field data after rollout — lab results explain a number, field data decides whether users are still affected (https://web.dev/articles/optimize-inp). The strongest distractor is the shotgun one: memoizing everything and deferring everything changes many variables in a single move, so a green number afterwards would not say which change did it, and INP is input delay plus handler work plus presentation, so memoization attacks at most one third of that while adding its own overhead. 'Not reproducible locally' is a fact about your machine, not about the users, and the desktop-only report hides exactly the segment that failed: a site-wide number can pass while checkout on mobile is failing.

mcqs.question: Product asks for the offline banner copy: 'Your changes will sync automatically within 5 minutes of reconnecting.' What is the most accurate engineering response?
options: We can queue and retry the writes, but not promise a time: retries are limited, the worker can be stopped, periodic sync is browser-scheduled.
Yes: once the device is back online, Background Sync guarantees delivery, so a five-minute window is a safe promise.
Yes, if we register a periodic background sync at a five-minute interval, since the platform honours that schedule.
No: the service worker is tied to the tab, so queued writes can only be replayed while the app is still open.
mcqs.explanation: Background Sync is a request to the browser, not a schedule: retries are limited, an attempt can be cut short, and the service worker can be stopped at any moment, while periodic background sync is browser-controlled and not available everywhere — so the honest copy states what is saved on this device and that sync will be attempted when possible, with pending items visible in the UI (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Progressive_web_apps/Guides/Offline_and_background_operation). The strongest distractor is the periodic-sync one, because it names the API that sounds purpose-built for 'every five minutes': the interval is the shortest gap the browser may leave between attempts, not a deadline it guarantees, and the API is missing on some platforms, so the same banner would lie on part of the fleet. 'Guarantees delivery' invents a guarantee the platform does not offer: a retry is best effort and an item can stay pending indefinitely. 'Tied to the tab' gets the mechanism backwards — the worker is a separate context with its own lifetime, which is what makes background work possible at all; the real constraint is that the platform may never schedule the run, so replaying from the next open tab is the fallback to design alongside it.

mcqs.question: Stakeholders want the same one-tap install prompt flow on iPhone that Chrome shows on Android. What is accurate?
options: On iOS and iPadOS there is no install prompt or install API: the user adds the app from the share menu, so the guidance has to be platform-specific.
Safari fires `beforeinstallprompt` like Chrome, so the existing handler only needs to be moved behind a visible button.
iOS supports the prompt only when the manifest declares `display: standalone`, a 512px icon and a start URL in scope.
iOS gates the prompt behind a paid Apple Developer account, so the flow only exists for apps registered there.
mcqs.explanation: The install entry point is not a uniform web capability: on Android and desktop Chrome the page can trigger its own prompt from `beforeinstallprompt`, while iOS and iPadOS have no install API — the user goes to Share, then Add to Home Screen, which makes the flow guidance you render rather than a button you call, and `display-mode: standalone` (or `navigator.standalone`) is how you detect the installed state afterwards (https://web.dev/learn/pwa/installation). The strongest distractor keeps `beforeinstallprompt`, because that is exactly what a Chrome-shaped implementation listens for and it never fires in Safari, so the button it unlocks is never enabled — a broken funnel that still passes a code review. The manifest option inverts cause and effect: `display`, `icons` and `start_url` describe the installed experience and influence Android's criteria; they do not create an entry point on iOS, where no published criteria exist at all. The developer-account option fails at the first manual install, because the share-menu path needs no account, no signing and no registration, which is why missing guidance rather than licensing is what breaks the iOS funnel.

mcqs.question: A hero section uses `min-height: 100vh` and its call to action sits at the bottom. On a phone the CTA loads underneath the expanded browser toolbar, and on a notched device it is half hidden by the home indicator. Product accepts a full-bleed hero but rejects any layout that moves while the user scrolls. Which implementation satisfies both constraints?
options: `min-height: 100svh` plus `padding-block-end: env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` on the hero.
`min-height: 100dvh` plus `padding-block-end: env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` on the hero.
`min-height: 100vh` plus a fixed `padding-block-end: 64px` to clear the browser toolbar.
`html, body { height: 100vh }` with `min-height: 100%` on the hero, so the percentage chain resolves against the viewport.
mcqs.explanation: `svh` is the small viewport unit: it is sized as if the browser controls were expanded, so the CTA starts inside the visible area and the value does not change when the toolbar collapses, while the inset padding keeps the bottom edge clear of the home indicator (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/length, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/env). The strongest distractor is the `dvh` version: it measures the viewport as it currently is, so it also fixes the initial clipping and would pass a screenshot review, but it re-resolves as the toolbar expands and collapses during scrolling — exactly the movement product excluded — and inside a scrollable hero that resize can also feed back into scroll position. Fixed `64px` padding is a constant tuned to one browser's toolbar on one device, so it is wrong on another UI state and says nothing about the notch, and the `height: 100%` chain only resolves back to the same oversized `100vh` that produced the clipped hero.

mcqs.question: A product card exposes its Edit and Delete actions with `.card:hover .actions { display: block }`. QA finds that on phones the buttons cannot be reached at all, and keyboard users cannot tab past the card title. What is the correct fix?
options: Keep the actions in the DOM and reachable — a persistent row or an explicit actions/menu button — restrict the hover styling to `@media (hover: hover)`, and keep a `:focus-visible` indicator on the controls.
Add `@media (hover: none) { .card:hover .actions { display: block } }` so touch devices reveal the actions on tap.
Replace the selector with `.card:focus-within .actions { display: block }` so focus is what reveals the actions.
Check `navigator.maxTouchPoints > 0` once at startup and add a class that shows the actions permanently on touch devices.
mcqs.explanation: Hover has to be an enhancement, and the media features exist to scope it: `hover` describes whether the primary input can hover comfortably and `pointer: coarse` describes an imprecise pointer such as a finger, so the hover styling belongs behind `@media (hover: hover)` while the action itself stays a real button that exists in the DOM, sits in the tab order and carries a `:focus-visible` ring (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/hover, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/pointer). The strongest distractor is the `hover: none` variant: it looks like the textbook use of the media feature, and it seems to work on some phones because a tap can leave an emulated sticky hover, but the actions remain `display: none` until that emulation happens, so they stay out of the accessibility tree and out of the keyboard tab order — the second half of the bug is untouched. `:focus-within` cannot bootstrap itself for the same reason: the controls inside are still `display: none` and therefore not focusable, so focus never enters the card. A one-time `maxTouchPoints` check samples hardware at page load rather than the primary input in use, so a touchscreen laptop driven by a mouse takes the touch branch and the styling stops matching the device people are actually using.

mcqs.question: A signup form ships the phone field as `<input type="number" inputMode="numeric" placeholder="Phone">`. On iOS the leading `+` cannot be typed, values containing spaces end up empty, and autofill never offers the saved number. Which change fixes the causes?
options: Add `inputMode="tel"`: inputmode overrides the control's type, so the keypad and the accepted characters both change without editing the type.

Use `type="tel"` with `autocomplete="tel"` and a real `<label>`; keep `inputmode` as an optional keypad hint and state the format rule explicitly, because the tel state performs no automatic format check.
Use `type="text"` with `inputMode="numeric"` and `pattern="[0-9]*"`, the documented way to request a numeric keypad while keeping a text field.
Keep `type="number"` and add `pattern="[+0-9 ()-]*"` so the value is validated instead of sanitized.
mcqs.explanation: The control's semantics come from `type`, the keypad is only a hint from `inputmode`, and autofill needs matching `autocomplete` tokens: `type="tel"` is the state for a telephone number, it is explicitly not validated to any particular format, so the rule is written separately, and `autocomplete="tel"` is what allows the saved number to be offered (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/input.html#telephone-state-(type=tel), https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Attributes/autocomplete). The original type is wrong for a second reason: the number state is documented as inappropriate for input that only happens to consist of digits — phone numbers, postal codes and card numbers are the spec's own examples — because it applies numeric value sanitization and a spinbox model the data does not have (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/input.html#number-state-(type=number)). The strongest distractor is the `type="text"` + `inputMode="numeric"` + `pattern="[0-9]*"` recipe: it is genuinely the documented pattern for digit-only values, but a phone number is not digit-only — it needs `+`, spaces and separators in many countries — so that pattern rejects exactly the input the example invites, and it still supplies no autocomplete token. Adding `inputMode="tel"` alone changes nothing structural, because inputmode never alters the type: the number state keeps sanitizing the value and no autofill token appears. Adding `pattern` to the number field also fails: the number state sanitizes before constraint validation runs, so a value the sanitizer has already emptied cannot be rescued, and `pattern` does not apply to the number state in the first place (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Attributes/pattern).

scenarios.prompt: This drag handle works with a mouse on desktop but misbehaves on touch: the browser sometimes scrolls instead of dragging, fast drags lose the element, and after a failed drag the handle stays stuck until the next tap. Find the bugs and rewrite the interaction.
rubric: Names `touch-action` as the declaration that claims the gesture before it starts, and says why cancelling inside the pointer handlers does not stop panning.
Calls `setPointerCapture` on `pointerdown` and releases it in a single ending path used by both `pointerup` and `pointercancel`.

Explains the stuck handle from the code: without capture `pointerup` outside the element never fires, so the leaked `pointermove` listener keeps moving the element (and a repeat press adds a second listener).
Guards the handler set — one `pointerId`, listeners removed in `end()` and in the unmount cleanup — instead of only removing `pointermove`.
Keeps a keyboard or button alternative for the gesture and validates with mouse, pen and touch.

scenarios.prompt: Review this service worker for a PWA that must show reasonably fresh data and safely sync user edits made offline. What does it get wrong, and how should the offline behavior be designed instead?
scenarios.modelAnswer: The fetch handler applies cache-first to every API request. Cache-first favors speed but serves potentially stale assets, so API data cached once is replayed indefinitely: users see old data even when online, with no freshness signal and no fallback policy. The fix is a per-resource strategy: network-first for API data, falling back to the cache when the network fails, and cache-first only where staleness is acceptable, such as versioned static assets. The UI should also expose freshness, so cached responses are presented as what they are. The sync handler has the more dangerous bugs. First, replay is not idempotent: if a POST reaches the server but the response is lost, or the sync is retried, the same edit is applied twice. Each queued operation needs an idempotency mechanism so replaying it cannot duplicate the side effect. Second, there is no conflict policy: the server may have newer state from another device, and the code has no defined outcome for that collision; conflict resolution must be decided before queued mutations are enabled. Third, the loop is all-or-nothing: one failed fetch rejects the waitUntil, the remaining operations never run, and because browsers limit Background Sync retries and execution time, and the service worker can be stopped between attempts, the queue can strand. Each operation should be attempted and persisted independently, with per-op error handling. Finally, the product copy around this must never promise that a background task will run at a particular time: periodic sync is browser-controlled, retries are limited, and the UI must tolerate failure while showing what is saved locally and what is pending sync.
rubric: Rejects cache-first for API data and chooses a per-resource strategy, network-first for freshness with cache fallback
Identifies non-idempotent replay as the critical safety bug and requires idempotent writes
Requires a defined conflict resolution policy before queued mutations are enabled
Makes the sync loop per-operation and tolerant of partial failure instead of all-or-nothing
Refuses to promise background execution timing in the UI and exposes pending-sync state

scenarios.prompt: This product grid passes review at 375px and 768px, where nothing overflows, and is reported wrong everywhere else: in a 500px split-screen pane the row overflows and the page scrolls sideways; at 390px the card still occupies 260px, leaving about a quarter of the row empty while product names wrap to four lines; at 900px the two cards cover 536px and the rest of the page is dead space. The stylesheet below is the only layout rule that applies. Redesign the responsive approach and describe how you would validate it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The layout has exactly two inputs: a 260px track and a 480px breakpoint. Every width above 480 therefore resolves to the same 536px row — at 390px that is a card plus dead margins on both sides and a title wrapping to four lines, at 900px it is a 536px island centred in the page, and between roughly 481px and 570px it is 536px of tracks inside less than that of content box, which is the sideways scroll. Note what is *not* broken: at 375 and 768 the row fits, which is precisely why snapshot review passed. The bug is that the component answers one question ("is there room for two 260px cards?") with a constant instead of with the space it was given. **Let the container decide the column count.** Replace the fixed tracks with an intrinsic one and drop both the media query and the centering that produce the dead columns: `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(260px, 1fr))`. The column count then follows the available width continuously — a 900px row gets three columns instead of a centred island, a 500px pane gets one wide card instead of an overflow, and no breakpoint has to be guessed. Use `auto-fit` when fewer cards than columns should stretch to fill the row; `auto-fill` keeps the empty tracks, which is the right choice only when a stable column rhythm matters more than filling. **Keep what is already right.** The `` carries `width={960} height={720}`, which reserves the 4:3 box before the image loads, and CSS `width: 100%; height: auto` makes it scale — that combination is the correct one and should survive the redesign, because removing the attributes is how a grid like this starts shifting as images arrive. **Fix the cramped card as a content problem, not a width problem.** A 260px card that wraps a product name to four lines needs wrapping over truncation, a `clamp()` type scale or a slightly larger minimum track; increasing the minimum in `minmax()` is the lever, not another breakpoint. **Give the card its own seam if it is reused.** If the same card also appears in a sidebar or a modal, a container query (`container-type: inline-size` on the wrapper plus `@container (min-width: 480px)`) is the correct test, because the card's constraint is its container, not the viewport. **Validation is the part that failed.** Test narrow, wide and intermediate widths in both orientations — including the awkward ones (390 portrait, 500 split pane, 844 landscape, 900, 1200) — with real content: long product names, a missing image, an odd card count, and 200% zoom. Check that the whole card link keeps a target of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels (WCAG 2.5.8) and that no width produces horizontal scrolling. Then read field data segmented by mobile instead of one aggregate, because a site-wide score can pass while the narrow layout is the one users get.
rubric: Diagnoses the fixed 260px tracks plus a single 480px breakpoint as the cause, and explains why 375/768 passing hid it.
Replaces the fixed tracks with an intrinsic track (`repeat(auto-fit, minmax(260px, 1fr))` or an equivalent flex/percentage solution) and removes the centering that produced the dead columns.
Keeps the declared image `width`/`height` for aspect ratio and makes the image fluid with CSS, rather than dropping the attributes.
Reaches for a container query when the card is reused in a container narrower than the viewport, instead of adding device breakpoints.
Validates between breakpoints in both orientations with real content and 200% zoom, and segments field data by device.

scenarios.prompt: This checkout form passes desktop QA and fails on phones. Reports: the phone field opens a generic keyboard and autofill fills nothing; when a field is focused, or when an error is shown, the fixed header covers it; with the keyboard open the fixed Pay bar is unreachable or sits under the home indicator; and the `keyboardOpen` heuristic makes the page jump while scrolling. `error` is declared but nothing ever sets it, so validation feedback is never rendered next to a field. Identify the defects and rewrite the component.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Start with what the browser is allowed to decide for you. Every field is a bare text input with a placeholder: no `type`, no `autocomplete`, no label element, and only the card field carries an `inputmode`. That is why the keyboard is generic and autofill does nothing. Rewrite the controls from the data, not from the digits: the card number is not a number, so `type="text"` with `inputMode="numeric"`, `autoComplete="cc-number"` and an explicit digit pattern; the phone field is `type="tel"` with `autoComplete="tel"`, and because the tel state performs no automatic format validation its rule has to be stated explicitly; the email field is `type="email"` with `autoComplete="email"`. Each field gets a visible `<label for>`, each error gets an `id` referenced by `aria-describedby`. Keep `inputmode` what it is — a keypad hint that changes neither the control's semantics nor its validation — and remember it is the `autocomplete` token, not the type, that makes autofill offer the saved number.

Delete the `keyboardOpen` heuristic instead of tuning it. `window.screen.height` describes the screen, not the area the browser is showing, `window.innerHeight` changes for reasons that have nothing to do with the keyboard (toolbar collapse, rotation, split screen, a resized desktop window), and `- 150` is a constant calibrated on one device. The contract for this feature is the opposite of measuring: the focused field and the submit action must stay usable when the viewport changes, whatever changed it, and the layout must not depend on a JavaScript keyboard-height constant.

Fix the overlap with scroll padding rather than with a header-height constant inside the form. The header is `position: fixed`, so it is out of flow and the browser can scroll a focused or invalid field straight underneath it. Put `scroll-padding-block-start` at least as large as the header on the scrolling container (`html { scroll-padding-block-start: 5rem }`, or the form itself if it is the scroll container), so every scroll-into-view target lands below the header instead of behind it.

Fix the Pay bar as its own defect. A `position: fixed; bottom: 0` bar with no bottom inset padding is the element that ends up under the home indicator and behind the on-screen keyboard, and the React fix of adding 320px of padding to the form is what produces the jumping. Either keep the primary action in normal flow at the end of the form, or make a sticky bar pad its bottom edge with `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` and verify that the button is still reachable with the keyboard open — portrait and landscape, keyboard closed and open.

Close the error loop. `error` is declared but never set, so the only feedback is a server response that the component does not render, and it would appear at the top of the page far from the field it concerns. Validate on submit, render the message next to the offending field, associate it with `aria-describedby`, and move focus to the first invalid field; keep the label visible after typing, because a placeholder disappears exactly when the user needs it.

Then prove it with a real matrix: portrait and landscape, 200% zoom, autofill from a saved profile, keyboard open and closed, installed mode, on real iOS and Android hardware. Check that every control keeps a `:focus-visible` indicator and a target of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, and that no fixed edge is left unpadded.
rubric: Chooses semantics per field (tel for the phone, email for the email, text plus a numeric keypad hint for the card number) and can say why `inputmode` is only a hint while `autocomplete` tokens drive autofill.
Removes the `innerHeight` / `screen.height` keyboard heuristic instead of tuning the constant, and explains that the layout must tolerate viewport changes without measuring a keyboard height.
Keeps the focused field clear of the fixed header by putting `scroll-padding` on the scroll container, and keeps the submit action usable while the keyboard is open.
Handles the fixed bar and the home indicator with `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` or moves the primary action into normal flow, instead of padding the form by a guessed pixel amount.

Closes the error path — visible labels, an inline message tied to the field with `aria-describedby`, focus moved to the first invalid field — and names a real-device test matrix rather than one emulator pass.
